stem: A 34-year-old with gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for 4 months. She reports galactorrhea and missed periods. Pregnancy test is negative and prolactin is elevated. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Primary hypothyroidism from an undetected drug interaction
options.B: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine, the brake on prolactin
options.C: Metoclopramide stimulates dopamine, raising prolactin release
options.D: A prolactinoma that now needs cabergoline twice weekly
options.E: Estrogen excess raising thyroid-binding globulin levels

why: Dopamine is the brake on prolactin. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide block dopamine, so prolactin rises.

whys.A: Nothing here points to thyroid drugs or disease.
whys.C: Dopamine inhibits prolactin; the drug blocks it.
whys.D: A drug cause must be excluded first; she takes a dopamine blocker.
whys.E: That changes levothyroxine needs, not prolactin.

stem: A 41-year-old with untreated Graves disease arrives with fever 40°C, heart rate 158, agitation and vomiting after an infection. Propranolol has been given. Which sequence is correct for the next drugs?

options.A: Iodine now, PTU 1 hour after it, plus hydrocortisone
options.B: PTU now, iodine an hour after it, plus hydrocortisone
options.C: Methimazole now, with levothyroxine held until afterwards
options.D: PTU now, aspirin for the fever, then iodine an hour later
options.E: Hydrocortisone alone, since it blocks all hormone release

why: Beta-blocker and PTU come first; iodine is given only after PTU because iodine first would feed new hormone synthesis. Steroids blunt peripheral conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency. Aspirin is avoided.

whys.A: Iodine before PTU supplies substrate for new hormone.
whys.C: The storm sequence taught is PTU first, then iodine.
whys.D: Aspirin frees bound hormone and is avoided in storm.
whys.E: Steroids help conversion and adrenal cover; they are added.

stem: An 81-year-old on metformin has A1c above goal. She lives alone and has fallen twice this year. Which add-on fits the lecture's reasoning?

options.A: Sitagliptin, because its hypoglycemia risk is low
options.B: Semaglutide plus sitagliptin, to cover both incretin steps
options.C: Repaglinide, because mealtime dosing prevents all lows
options.D: Pioglitazone, because fluid retention protects from falls
options.E: Glipizide, because it is the most potent oral option

why: For an older adult who falls, choose the safest drug, not the most potent. Sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release; a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable.

whys.B: A GLP-1 RA is not combined with a DPP-4 inhibitor.
whys.D: Fluid retention and heart failure are its risks.
whys.E: Sulfonylureas carry the highest oral hypoglycemia risk.

stem: A 55-year-old on basal-bolus insulin starts metoprolol after a myocardial infarction. Which counseling point is most important?

options.A: Glucagon no longer works, so only dextrose can be used
options.B: Hypoglycemia cannot occur on a beta-blocker, so relax targets
options.C: Metoprolol causes euglycemic DKA, so hold insulin when ill
options.D: Warning symptoms may be masked; check glucose, rule of 15
options.E: Metoprolol raises insulin levels, so halve every insulin dose

why: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia warning symptoms. Treat a low with 15 g of carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes; glucagon or dextrose rescue severe hypoglycemia.

whys.A: Both remain rescue options for severe lows.
whys.B: It can occur and may go unnoticed.
whys.E: The taught effect is masking, not a level change.

stem: A 49-year-old taking tamoxifen after breast cancer is started on paroxetine for depression and hot flashes. Which concern should the PA raise?

options.A: Tamoxifen inhibits CYP2D6 and raises paroxetine levels
options.B: The pair causes hyperkalemia, so potassium is monitored
options.C: Paroxetine induces CYP3A4 and clears tamoxifen faster
options.D: Paroxetine adds to tamoxifen's endometrial cancer risk
options.E: Paroxetine inhibits CYP2D6 and blunts tamoxifen activation

why: Tamoxifen needs CYP2D6 to be activated. Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6, so less active drug is formed.

whys.A: Cinacalcet is the CYP2D6 inhibitor in this unit.
whys.C: The taught interaction is CYP2D6 inhibition.
whys.D: That risk belongs to tamoxifen alone.

stem: A 66-year-old has taken finasteride for 2 years. His screening PSA is 2.4 ng/mL. How should this value be read?

options.A: As uninterpretable, so PSA screening should stop
options.B: As about 4.8 ng/mL, because finasteride halves PSA
options.C: As about 1.2 ng/mL, because finasteride doubles PSA
options.D: As about 4.8 ng/mL, because testosterone raises PSA
options.E: As 2.4 ng/mL, because finasteride does not change PSA

why: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half, so the measured value is doubled when screening.

whys.A: The value is still usable once doubled.
whys.C: It lowers PSA; the correction is to double.
whys.D: He is on finasteride, not testosterone.
whys.E: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half.

stem: A 39-year-old with Cushing syndrome and type 2 diabetes starts mifepristone. A month later her glucose control is better, but serum cortisol is higher than before. Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: Expected: also check PSA, which the drug lowers by half
options.B: Adrenal crisis: give IV hydrocortisone and fluids now
options.C: Expected with receptor block: follow clinically, check K⁺
options.D: Treatment failure: switch to ketoconazole to lower cortisol
options.E: Lab error: cortisol always falls on a receptor blocker

why: Mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor. Cortisol levels rise, so response is judged clinically. It causes hypokalemia and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

whys.B: She is improving; nothing suggests crisis.
whys.D: Cortisol rises with receptor blockade; levels mislead.

discriminator: Synthesis blockers lower cortisol; a receptor blocker does not.

stem: A 24-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive starts rifampin for 4 months. She asks whether her pill still works. Which advice is correct?

options.A: Double the pill dose and no backup method is needed
options.B: Switch to levothyroxine timing rules: separate by 4 hours
options.C: No change is needed; only St. John's wort matters
options.D: Rifampin raises estrogen levels; watch for clots instead
options.E: Rifampin lowers hormone levels; use backup contraception

why: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort) lower contraceptive efficacy; use backup contraception.

whys.A: The lecture's answer is backup contraception.
whys.B: Separation fixes binding, not enzyme induction.
whys.C: Rifampin is a named inducer, as is St. John's wort.

discriminator: Induction lowers levels; it cannot be fixed by spacing doses.

stem: A 45-year-old on a stable prednisone dose for sarcoidosis starts itraconazole for a fungal infection. Three weeks later she has new facial rounding, glucose 230 mg/dL and insomnia. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.A: The azole displaces steroid from thyroid-binding globulin
options.B: Prednisone inhibits azole clearance, causing azole toxicity
options.C: The azole induces CYP3A4, speeding steroid clearance
options.D: The azole inhibits CYP3A4, raising corticosteroid exposure
options.E: The azole blocks cortisol synthesis, causing deficiency

why: Azole antifungals raise corticosteroid exposure through CYP3A4. Same dose, more effect: hyperglycemia and cushingoid features.

whys.A: That protein is about estrogen and levothyroxine.
whys.B: The taught interaction runs the other way.
whys.C: Induction would lower steroid effect; rifampin does that.
whys.E: Her findings are steroid excess, not deficiency.

discriminator: Inhibitors raise steroid exposure; rifampin, phenytoin and carbamazepine lower it.

stem: A 29-year-old started methimazole 5 weeks ago for Graves disease. She calls with fever of 38.9°C and a severe sore throat for one day. Which instruction is correct?

options.A: Switch to PTU today since it has the lower liver risk
options.B: Stop methimazole now and come in for a CBC today
options.C: Add iodine solution to block hormone release tonight
options.D: Continue methimazole and check TSH in 6–8 weeks
options.E: Continue methimazole and take aspirin for the fever

why: Both thionamides carry agranulocytosis and liver warnings. Fever or sore throat on a thionamide means stop the drug and check a CBC.

whys.A: PTU has the greater liver risk and shares agranulocytosis.
whys.C: Iodine is a thyroid-storm step, not for this warning sign.
whys.D: TSH timing does not address possible agranulocytosis.
whys.E: Fever or sore throat means stop and check a CBC.

discriminator: Agranulocytosis: both drugs. Worse liver risk: PTU.

stem: A 57-year-old on empagliflozin has had vomiting and poor intake for 2 days. Glucose is 168 mg/dL, bicarbonate is low and ketones are positive. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Euglycemic DKA; the drug is held during illness
options.B: Not DKA, because the glucose is under 250 mg/dL
options.C: Pancreatitis from the drug; check for gallstones
options.D: Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia; treat with the rule of 15
options.E: Lactic acidosis from metformin; stop it for contrast

why: SGLT2 inhibitors cause genital yeast infections, volume depletion and euglycemic DKA. They are held when the patient is ill or before surgery.

whys.B: SGLT2 inhibitors cause DKA with near-normal glucose.
whys.C: Pancreatitis and gallstones are GLP-1 RA concerns.
whys.D: Glucose is 168 and she is not on a sulfonylurea.
whys.E: She takes empagliflozin and has ketones.

stem: A 63-year-old with SIADH from small-cell lung cancer has sodium 122 mEq/L and mild nausea. No therapy has been tried. Which plan matches the lecture's order of therapy?

options.A: Give fludrocortisone and monitor blood pressure and potassium
options.B: Start demeclocycline first because it has the fewest risks
options.C: Start desmopressin and limit fluids to prevent water loss
options.D: Start tolvaptan at home and recheck sodium in two weeks
options.E: Restrict fluids; tolvaptan in hospital if refractory

why: Fluid restriction is first-line for SIADH. Tolvaptan or demeclocycline are for refractory cases; tolvaptan can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and injure the liver, so it starts in hospital.

whys.A: That is mineralocorticoid replacement, not SIADH care.
whys.B: It causes photosensitivity and nephrotoxicity; not first.
whys.D: It is started in hospital because it can overcorrect.

stem: A 58-year-old has taken prednisone daily for 8 months for polymyalgia. He ran out 4 days ago. He presents with vomiting, weakness and blood pressure 82/50. What explains this, and what is the treatment?

options.A: Axis recovered within days; restart oral prednisone at home
options.B: Steroid excess causing hyperglycemia; give insulin and fluids
options.C: Suppressed ACTH, no cortisol reserve; IV hydrocortisone
options.D: Rebound ACTH surge overdriving the adrenal; give ketoconazole
options.E: Mineralocorticoid excess from prednisone; give spironolactone

why: Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH and the adrenal shrinks. Stopping abruptly leaves the axis unable to make cortisol: adrenal crisis, treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids. Prevention is a taper.

whys.A: Recovery takes time; crisis needs IV therapy.
whys.B: He stopped the steroid; this is deficiency.
whys.D: ACTH is suppressed, and the adrenal has shrunk.

discriminator: Crisis = too little cortisol after suppression.

stem: A 78-year-old with coronary artery disease and new hypothyroidism (TSH 14 mIU/L) is starting levothyroxine. Which plan is safest?

options.A: Start a low dose and recheck TSH at 6–8 weeks
options.B: Start a low dose taken with calcium at breakfast
options.C: Start a full dose and recheck TSH in 1 week
options.D: Start a full dose and titrate to a suppressed TSH
options.E: Delay treatment until the TSH rises above 20 mIU/L

why: Start low in older adults and in cardiac disease, then check TSH at 6–8 weeks. Over-replacement causes tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and bone loss.

whys.B: Calcium reduces absorption; separate by 4 hours.
whys.C: Older and cardiac patients start low; TSH needs 6–8 weeks.
whys.D: Over-replacement risks tachycardia, AF and bone loss.
whys.E: The lecture teaches start low, not withhold.

takeaway: Old or cardiac: start low, TSH at 6–8 weeks.
discriminator: Under-treating is slow; over-replacing hits the heart and bone.

stem: A 62-year-old on dialysis starts cinacalcet for secondary hyperparathyroidism. Two weeks later she has tingling around the mouth and muscle cramps. Which lab and which added risk go with this drug?

options.A: Low potassium; cinacalcet also causes gynecomastia
options.B: High calcium; a thiazide should be added to lower it
options.C: Low sodium; cinacalcet also retains free water
options.D: Low calcium; cinacalcet also prolongs the QT interval
options.E: High calcium; cinacalcet also causes hypercalciuria

why: Cinacalcet lowers PTH secretion. Adverse effects are nausea, hypocalcemia and QT prolongation, so calcium is monitored. Calcitriol and PTH replacement carry the opposite risk.

whys.A: That mixes mifepristone and spironolactone effects.
whys.B: Thiazides raise calcium; loops lower it.
whys.E: Those are the calcitriol and PTH-replacement risks.

discriminator: Cinacalcet → low calcium; calcitriol → high calcium.

stem: A 60-year-old on repaglinide with meals starts gemfibrozil for triglycerides. A week later he has sweating and tremor before lunch on several days. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2D6, as cinacalcet also does
options.B: Gemfibrozil masks hypoglycemia like a beta-blocker does
options.C: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and raises repaglinide levels
options.D: Gemfibrozil induces CYP2C8 and lowers repaglinide levels
options.E: Gemfibrozil blocks DPP-4, doubling the incretin effect

why: Gemfibrozil raises repaglinide levels through CYP2C8, so the secretagogue effect, and hypoglycemia, increase.

whys.B: He has symptoms; they are not masked.
whys.E: It is not an incretin drug.

stem: A 71-year-old started desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus 10 days ago. To 'stay hydrated' he drinks water all day. He is now confused with a headache and nausea. Which step is most appropriate first?

options.A: Start demeclocycline to counter the retained water
options.B: Raise the desmopressin dose for incomplete control
options.C: Add tolvaptan to speed water excretion at home
options.D: Check serum sodium for desmopressin hyponatremia
options.E: Check liver tests for desmopressin hepatotoxicity

why: Desmopressin keeps free water in. The risk is hyponatremia, so sodium is monitored and fluids are limited.

whys.B: More drug would retain more water.
whys.C: Tolvaptan is for SIADH and is started in hospital.
whys.E: Liver injury is the tolvaptan concern.

discriminator: Desmopressin → hyponatremia; tolvaptan → overcorrection and liver injury.

stem: A patient with acromegaly switches from octreotide to pegvisomant. Three months later IGF-1 is normal, but MRI shows the adenoma unchanged in size. Which statement explains both findings?

options.A: It blocks the GH receptor: IGF-1 falls, tumor untouched
options.B: It replaces GH, so feedback switches the adenoma off
options.C: It lowers GH release, so the tumor should shrink with time
options.D: It blocks IGF-1 itself, so GH and the tumor are suppressed
options.E: It restores dopamine tone, so prolactin and GH both fall

why: Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor, so the liver makes less IGF-1. It does not act on the pituitary, so it does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 and liver tests.

whys.B: Somatropin replaces GH and is for deficiency.
whys.D: Its target is the GH receptor, not IGF-1.

takeaway: Pegvisomant fixes the lab, not the tumor.
discriminator: Octreotide lowers GH release; pegvisomant blocks its receptor.

stem: A 48-year-old on a stable levothyroxine dose has TSH 9.8 mIU/L. She takes it every morning with breakfast, her calcium carbonate and a new iron tablet. She has not missed a dose. What is the best next step?

options.A: Stop the iron permanently because the two can never be combined
options.B: Switch to methimazole because the levothyroxine has failed
options.C: Take it on an empty stomach, 4 h from calcium and iron
options.D: Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 2 weeks
options.E: Move the dose to dinner so it is taken with the largest meal

why: Calcium, iron and antacids reduce levothyroxine absorption. Take it 30–60 minutes before breakfast and separate those products by at least 4 hours, then check TSH at 6–8 weeks.

whys.A: They can be combined when separated by 4 hours.
whys.D: Fix absorption first; TSH is rechecked at 6–8 weeks.
whys.E: Food reduces absorption; it is taken on an empty stomach.

stem: A 52-year-old with acromegaly has taken octreotide for a year. IGF-1 is at goal. He now reports episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals and a resting pulse of 52. Which explanation fits best?

options.A: Cabergoline effect: orthostatic hypotension and nausea
options.B: Pegvisomant toxicity: liver injury needing liver tests
options.C: Tumor growth: the pituitary mass is pressing locally
options.D: Desmopressin effect: hyponatremia from retained water
options.E: Expected octreotide effects: gallstones and bradycardia

why: Octreotide and lanreotide cause GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia (and glucose changes). Biliary pain plus a slow pulse in a controlled patient is the drug, not the disease.

whys.A: Those are dopamine-agonist effects, not his drug.
whys.B: He takes octreotide; liver tests are the pegvisomant concern.
whys.C: IGF-1 is at goal and the symptoms are biliary.
whys.D: He is not on desmopressin and has no sodium symptoms.
